Third Conditional in Negative Form
We use the third conditional or the unreal past conditional in the negative form to talk about the imaginary results of actions that didn't happen.

We use the third conditional in negative statements when we want to talk about the results of an action that could have been avoided, but it wasn’t.

Take a look at the following structure to describe an unreal situation that we cannot change:



If+ subject + had not/ hadn’t + main verb in past participle + complement +comma (,) + subject + would not/ wouldn’t have + main verb in past participle + complement

 

Example: 

If I hadn’t used the function to count the characters, I wouldn’t have known the number of characters in the string.

 

Remember that you can reverse the clauses. Doing this will not change the meaning of the sentence and you won’t need to add a comma to separate them.

 Example:

I wouldn’t have known the number of characters in the string if I hadn’t used the function to count the characters.

 

On the other hand, the third conditional in negative form can have the negative connotation just in one of the two clauses, either the if-clause or the result clause. However, the meaning can change. Look at the following statements:

Examples:

If I had known that PHP was so useful for designing web pages, I wouldn’t have wasted my time looking for other programs.

(In this case, the person regrets that he didn’t know about PHP, so he wasted his time looking for other programs. He is upset.)

 

If I hadn’t known that PHP was so useful for designing web pages, I would have wasted my time looking for other programs.

(In this case, the person imagines a hypothetical situation. If he hadn’t known about PHP, he would have wasted his time. Fortunately, it didn’t happen, so he is pleased.)
If I hadn't been studying PHP for the last year, I wouldn't have known about the importance of these topics for our career.
If I hadn't asked the teacher about the functions of strings, he wouldn't have told me that the people who created PHP had several functions for strings created.
Causative with Have
We use the causative with the verb have when we want to talk about something that someone has done for us or for another person.

When using “have” as a causative you say that an action was done but you didn’t do it yourself, instead, you asked or requested it to be done by someone else.

There are two ways to use “have” as a causative:

 

In the first one, you don’t need to mention who did the action. Use the following structure if you want to do it this way:

 

Subject + have (you can use any tense) + object + main verb in past participle

 

Example: 

I have my scripts reviewed every time I’m done with one of them.

(In this case, we don’t know who the reviewer is.)

 

 The second way to use “have” as a causative is by mentioning the person who did the action. You can use the following structure:

 

Subject + have (you can use any tense) + agent (who does the action) + main verb in base form + object

 

Example:

I had John write my script using strings.
I'll have you answer some questions at the end.
The creators had this function reverse the string.

images.text: Professor Adams had me prepare this presentation, so I have to tell you about my experience with Strings and Constants in PHP. Pay close attention because if I hadn't been studying PHP for the last year, I wouldn't have known about the importance of these topics for our career; and, besides, I'll have you answer some questions at the end. For starters, I'll give you a brief definition and some examples. I found out that strings are a series of characters put together; like in a sequence of elements that use some character encoding. Some of them are: Strrev(), Strlen(string), Ucwords(string), etc.

If I hadn't asked the teacher about the functions of strings, he wouldn't have told me that the people who created PHP had several functions for strings created. An example of a string function is “Strlen(string)”; this function gives you the length of the string itself. So, if you write “echo strlen(“Welcome to Cloudways”) the output will be “20”. Another example is the function Strev(string). The creators had this function reverse the string. So, by writing echo strrev(“Welcome to Cloudways”) the result will be “Welcome to Cloudways” backwards: “syawduolC ot emocleW”.

Now, I wouldn't have been able to identify what constants are if I hadn't read an online article, and I want to tell you a little bit about them too. Constants are identifiers for simple values that cannot change during the execution of the script, and they can be used across said script. Unlike normal variables, you don't need to use a “$” sign, so If you want to create a constant you can use the “define()” function.

I hope this information I just gave you is useful. Now, I'm going to ask you some questions, I hope you're ready!
